title: Structs vs Classes and Design Practice
learningObjectives: Compare struct and class defaults and typical use.
Recognize that both can contain methods and constructors.
Choose simple public records versus encapsulated classes.
Design object interfaces that preserve invariants.
Apply composition and encapsulation in a small model.

understand.concept: struct and class differ in default member access and default inheritance access; otherwise they share core capabilities. Use type design to clarify data and behavior.
understand.whyItMatters: Knowing both forms prevents artificial distinctions and encourages clear interfaces.
understand.explain: Choose based on intended access defaults and design the API around responsibility, ownership and invariants.

examples.title: struct and class defaults
examples.explanation: struct defaults public access; class defaults private.

examples.title: Struct with methods
examples.code: struct Point{int x=0;int y=0;int sum()const{return x+y;};};
examples.explanation: struct can have member functions and defaults.

examples.title: Class with public interface
examples.code: class Counter{public:void add(){++value;}int get()const{return value;}private:int value=0;};
examples.explanation: class supports data and methods with explicit access control.

examples.title: Use type responsibly
examples.explanation: Simple data aggregates can be expressed with struct.

examples.title: Protect invariant
examples.code: class Positive{public:explicit Positive(int n):value(n){if(n<=0)throw std::invalid_argument(\"positive required\");}int get()const{return value;}private:int value;};
examples.explanation: Class can enforce a rule during construction.

practise.guidedTask: For Structs vs Classes and Design Practice, trace every example. List each type, object, member, initial value, access path, and state change. Identify where encapsulation or initialization affects correctness.
practise.independentTask: Create a small C++ model focused on Structs vs Classes and Design Practice (such as a Point, Student, Product, or Account). Include multiple objects, initialization, at least one operation/member access, and test normal, boundary and invalid states. Explain which fields should be public or private and why.
hints: Define the type and its responsibilities before creating objects.
Initialize members deliberately and trace their values.
Use dot for objects and arrow only for pointers.
Keep fields private when they must enforce rules.
Test object creation, valid operations and rejected updates.

questions.explanation: They differ mainly in default access.

questions.prompt: Can class hold data and methods?

questions.explanation: struct is commonly used for simple records.
Class can enforce invariants through its interface.
